title: Koko Eating Bananas
statement:
There are `piles.length` piles of bananas; pile `i` holds `piles[i]` bananas. A monkey has `h` hours before the keepers return.

The monkey picks one integer eating speed `k` (bananas per hour) and sticks to it. Each hour it chooses a single pile and eats `k` bananas from it; if the pile has fewer than `k` left, it finishes that pile and waits out the rest of the hour without starting another.

Return the **smallest** `k` that lets the monkey finish every pile within `h` hours. `h` is always at least `piles.length`, so an answer exists.

target.note: O(n log M) where M = max pile. M is capped at 10^9, so the binary search makes at most ~30 passes and the benchmark, which grows n with M fixed, sees linear growth

hints: If speed k is fast enough, is k + 1 fast enough too? What does that say about the set of speeds that work?
Feasibility is monotonic in k: false, false, ..., true, true. So binary search over the answer itself, between 1 and the largest pile, checking each candidate with one pass over the piles.
lo = 1, hi = max(piles). While lo < hi: mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; total the hours as the sum of ceil(pile / mid) in a long. If total <= h, hi = mid, else lo = mid + 1. Return lo.
followups: Can you tighten the initial search bounds, e.g. a lower bound of ceil(sum / h)?
Name another problem where you binary search on the answer — say, shipping packages within D days, or splitting an array to minimize the largest sum.
What changes if the monkey may move on to the next pile within the same hour?
explain: The question "can the monkey finish at speed k?" is monotonic: once a speed works, every faster speed works too. That turns the problem into finding the first true in a sorted boolean sequence, so binary search on k between 1 and max(piles) — no faster speed is ever needed, since at max(piles) each pile takes exactly one hour. Checking a speed is one pass summing ceil(p / k). Total time O(n log M) with M = max pile (about 30 checks for 10^9), O(1) extra space. Two Java traps: the hour total can reach 10^13 at low speeds, so sum it in a long; and (p + k - 1) / k overflows int when both are near 10^9, so use (p - 1) / k + 1 or long arithmetic. Trying k = 1, 2, 3, ... is O(n · answer), hopeless when the answer is in the hundreds of millions.
